note:
Colorado, from the department's own spreadsheet, DR_1098_Withholding_Calculator_Nov_2025_Revision_for_2026.xlsx, downloaded from its link on https://tax.colorado.gov/DR1098 on 13 November 2026 (served with Last-Modified 30 June 2026, SHA-256 7addcab146b9eeb9d3056016fbb5f4753488905fdfd19e91a07084ac6ba32cd0). The DR 1098 guide has no worked example, so the calculator is the only computation of Colorado's own there is. The book computes lines 1c, 2b, 2c, 2d and 2f by formula; lines 1a, 1b, 2a and 2e are typed in. Line 2a is typed as the book's own instruction on that line says, $5,500 for anyone but a joint filer and $11,000 for one, so these rows check the engine's choice of that amount against the instruction and its arithmetic against the formulas. The figures are what the book's formulas return for those inputs, computed by an Excel formula interpreter (the Python formulas package, which reads the formulas out of the file) because no spreadsheet program was at hand; the file carries no cached results.

The tolerance is half a cent because the book never rounds: line 2d is =J11/J5, the quotient as it falls, and line 2f adds line 2e to it. Every money cell is formatted "$"#,##0, so the sheet shows this row as $79, but that is a display format and not a rounding rule, and neither DR 1098 nor the Wage Withholding Tax Guide states one. The engine rounds the period's amount to the cent, so half a cent either side of the book's quotient is what agreement means. Rounding down instead lands a cent off the next two rows and fails both.

Three rows, one per filing status and pay period the engine treats differently: the single and head of household rows take the $5,500, the joint row the $11,000, and the three cover biweekly, monthly and weekly pay. A fourth row types line 2a from a DR 0004 instead (PAY-684). The additional amount on line 2e is not modelled, so no row reads it.

Circular M Rev. 12/25, percentage method, page 12, worked by hand from steps 1 to 6 (the circular prints no example at these wages): weekly $1,000, one exemption, week 26, the last before the year's FICA reaches $2,000
note: PAY-590. A calculation from the text of the method, not a worked example of the circular's own, so it adds nothing to the entry's verified status, which rests on the two rows above. The percentage method takes the Social Security and Medicare withheld in the period off the wages until the year's total reaches $2,000 and then discontinues the step. $1,000 a week withholds $62.00 and $14.50, so the year reaches $1,912.50 after 25 weeks, $1,989.00 after 26 and is past the cap after 27. Before the cap: (1,000 - 76.50 - 85) x 5% = 41.93; after it: (1,000 - 85) x 5% = 45.75. The circular prints the weekly exemption factor rounded to $85, the engine annualises and takes the annual $4,400, which is $84.62 a week, so it lands one and two cents above (41.94, 45.77): the tolerance is that rounding and nothing else. An even share of the cap, which the printed tables take, gives 43.85 in every week and fails both rows by nearly two dollars.
